reference.source: Rockwood and Green's Fractures in Adults
clinicalPearls: A distal radius fracture with volar (palmar) displacement and angulation of the distal fragment, the mirror image of a Colles fracture
It produces a characteristic garden-spade deformity of the wrist
The usual mechanism is a fall onto the dorsum of a flexed wrist or a direct blow to the back of the wrist
The pattern is inherently unstable, and volar angulation tends to recur after closed reduction
Volar plate fixation is often required, although stable or undisplaced patterns may be managed by closed reduction and plaster immobilisation
It should be distinguished from a volar Barton fracture, which is an intra-articular volar rim fracture-dislocation
Median nerve function must be assessed, as acute compression can occur
reference.pathophysiology: A force directed onto the dorsum of a flexed wrist, or a fall onto the back of the hand, fractures the distal radial metaphysis and displaces the distal fragment volarly, the opposite of the dorsal displacement seen in a Colles fracture. The pull of the forearm muscles and the inherent instability of the pattern tend to recreate volar angulation after reduction, so maintenance of reduction in plaster is difficult. Volar displacement can also crowd the carpal tunnel, threatening the median nerve, and articular extension of the fracture line predisposes to incongruity and later arthritis.
additionalDifferentials: Distal radial shaft or Galeazzi injury
Distal radial physeal injury in skeletally immature patients
additionalInvestigations: Posteroanterior and lateral wrist radiographs, the lateral showing volar tilt
Assessment of radial height, radial inclination and volar tilt
Examination and documentation of median nerve function
Post-reduction radiographs to confirm alignment and monitor for re-displacement
redFlags: Acute median nerve compression or carpal tunnel symptoms
Marked instability with loss of reduction
Intra-articular extension suggesting a volar Barton pattern
reference.prognosis: Because volar-displaced fractures are unstable and prone to re-displacement, many require operative fixation; anatomical volar plate fixation generally restores good function, whereas malunion causes deformity, weakness and median nerve symptoms.
pitfalls: Treating the injury as a stable Colles-type fracture and accepting loss of reduction
references: Rockwood and Green's Fractures in Adults
management: Anatomical reduction and volar locking-plate fixation for the typically unstable displaced pattern, as volar angulation tends to recur after closed reduction.
Closed reduction and well-moulded plaster immobilisation for stable or undisplaced fractures.
Assess and document median nerve function, with carpal tunnel decompression if there is progressive median nerve compromise.
Analgesia and early limb elevation to control pain and swelling.
Post-reduction and serial radiographs to confirm alignment and detect re-displacement.
Hand therapy and physiotherapy to restore wrist and finger range of motion and grip strength.
Refer to orthopaedic trauma for operative planning, particularly for intra-articular extension requiring precise reconstruction.
